proposed_text: A drinking-water laboratory method for counting particles and identifying subsampled materials by infrared spectroscopy. Source details California State Water Resources Control Board and SCCWRP. Official document. 2022. Official source Findings The procedure separates particle counting from chemical identification and requires blank controls and demonstrated laboratory performance. The method states a lowest reliably detected particle size of 50 µm . That is a method-scope value, not a safe exposure threshold. The procedure first counts objects by microscopy and then uses infrared spectroscopy on a representative selection to establish material identity. The confirmed proportion is applied to the microscopy count to estimate microplastic abundance. This is different from chemically identifying every object originally counted. The method also places sample collection outside its scope and limits validation to its stated particle-size range. Neither a filter fraction nor an instrument name establishes capability for all smaller particles. Source: PDF pp. 2-3, sections 1.0-2.0 . The document distinguishes controls according to the stage and question they address. Field blanks examine contamination associated with collection and transport; laboratory reagent blanks follow the analytical process; fortified blanks contain added particles to evaluate performance. These controls are complementary. A clean background result alone does not demonstrate recovery of particles, and successful recovery does not show that background contamination is absent. Interpreting an implemented method requires the corresponding control results and trained analytical work. Source: PDF pp. 3-4, section 3.0 Definitions . Methods and scope Revised May 27, 2022. PDF pp. 2–3 §§1–2: treated drinking water, microscopic counting plus IR identification, size-fraction processing, contamination controls and laboratory-specific reporting limits. What this source can support An official analytical procedure within its treated-water scope. Not a particle health threshold, packaging-release test, or assay for all nanoplastics. Spectroscopy on representative subsamples yields estimated confirmed counts. before_text: Multi-method fiber and additive characterization of commercial wet wipes purchased in the United Kingdom. Source details Tommaso Nacci, Francesca De Falco, Richard C. Thompson, Federico Vitale, Ilaria Degano, Francesca Modugno. Journal of Analytical and Applied Pyrolysis. 2025. DOI: 10.1016/j.jaap.2025.107200 Findings Conventional wipes contained polypropylene and/or polyethylene terephthalate together with cellulose. The investigated flushable and biodegradable groups were cellulose-based. Composition and organic additive signals were measured, not a release rate or infant dose. Methods and scope SEM characterized fiber morphology, ATR-FTIR assessed bulk composition, and evolved-gas MS plus multi-shot pyrolysis GC-MS separated additive and fiber signatures. Air-dried, previously unused wipe material was analyzed. No particle-release experiment or release-procedure blank series was reported because the endpoint was material composition. before_text: Aging and particle dynamics from cut pieces of nylon, polypropylene, and cellulose tea-bag materials in water. Source details Alexander A. Yaroslavov, Anna A. Efimova, Tatyana E. Grokhovskaya, Anastasiia G. Badikova, Vasily V. Spiridonov, Denis V. Pozdyshev, Sergey V. Lyulin, Jose M. Kenny. Polymers. 2025. DOI: 10.3390/polym17192700 Findings Bulk chemistry identified nylon, polypropylene, and cellulose bag materials. Particle sizes and concentrations evolved differently during soaking and subsequent aging. Cellulose-derived particles must remain separate from synthetic-plastic particles. Methods and scope Infrared spectroscopy, calorimetry, and thermogravimetry identified bulk materials. DLS followed hydrodynamic size; NTA measured suspended-particle concentration; laser electrophoresis measured mobility. Cut and rinsed bag squares were exposed in water under short and extended soaking/aging protocols. Distilled-water DLS control showed no scattering correlation. Experiments were replicated. What this source can support Useful mechanistic evidence that time, material, and size methodology affect observed particles, particularly below ordinary microscopy windows. Cut squares rather than intact retail bags. Some measurements followed prolonged heating/aging, not a normal cup preparation. Bulk polymer identity does not chemically identify every NTA-counted particle. Numerical NTA table resides in a supplement not reviewed here, so no exact count is reproduced. In-vitro findings do not establish consumer safety or clinical harm. Participants collected settled floor dust using household vacuum cleaners, and a questionnaire recorded features of their living spaces. That design links the recovered material to the sampled residences and collection procedure. It is not an air sampler measuring what a resident breathed. Differences between building or furnishing categories in this observational survey also do not isolate a single source, because the recorded household features were not controlled experimental exposures. Source: PDF p. 2, sections 2.1-2.2 . The chemical analysis used particles selected from sieved size fractions, while optical and electron microscopy described morphology. Composition among the selected particles is a different quantity from the total amount of dust, an airborne concentration or an inhaled dose. Cellulose and synthetic polymers must also remain distinct when interpreting the material categories. The source supports a description of the selected settled-dust samples, with the sampling and identification limits retained rather than extended to all indoor exposure. The clinical pilot changed its sampling procedure after examining the initial results. The later phase included washed placental tissue, tissue taken from the placental core and a collection of airborne fallout in the operating room. Materials used in delivery and preparation were also investigated. These comparisons are central to the study question: a signal in a clinical specimen must be considered alongside opportunities for contamination during collection and handling. Source: PDF p. 3, sections 2.1-2.2 Study Population and Sample Collecting . The discussion shows why the controls affect source attribution. Polymer findings in clinical materials and airborne fallout complicated the interpretation of signals in biological samples. A polymer that appeared informative in the initial phase could also be found in a possible contamination source examined later. The paper therefore supports attention to sampling and contamination control; this pilot does not establish population prevalence, a route from a particular consumer product or a demonstrated clinical consequence.
